title: Lost in the Sahara for 9 Days, He Drank Bat Blood #shorts
description:
Case 008. April 1994: Mauro Prosperi, an Italian police officer and pentathlete, was running the Marathon des Sables, a six-day race of about 250 km across the Moroccan Sahara. On 14 April, during the fourth and longest stage, a sandstorm hit and he lost the marked trail. A search helicopter flew over without seeing him. He sheltered in an abandoned Muslim shrine, where by his own account he killed bats and drank their blood, then walked toward distant mountains in the cool of early morning and evening, eating lizards and beetles. After about nine days a young girl herding goats found him; her Tuareg family gave him goat's milk and he was taken to hospital in Algeria, roughly 290 km (180 miles) from where he disappeared and many kilos lighter. He recovered and later went back to run the race again. Parts of his story have been questioned over the years, including by the race's organiser; Prosperi has always stood by it. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story.

source_notes: Read for this run: Wikipedia (Mauro Prosperi; it leans on a 1998 Men's Journal feature and a 2014 BBC interview), History.com ('5 Stunning Real-Life Survival Stories', updated 2025), RECOIL OFFGRID (Patrick McCarthy, 'Alone in the Sahara', 2018, which quotes the Men's Journal piece and Kenneth Kamler's book) and ExplorersWeb ('More Great Survival Stories', 2020). The BBC Magazine interview of November 2014 could not be opened by this run and is not used or listed; it is known here only second-hand. Agreed by the sources that mention each point: Italian police officer; the 1994 Marathon des Sables in Morocco, a six-day race (History), 251 km / 156 miles (Wikipedia, OffGrid; ExplorersWeb says 233 km, so the insert says 'ABOUT 250 KM'); he went astray on the fourth and longest stage, 14 April (Wikipedia, OffGrid); a sandstorm disoriented him and he kept moving in it (Wikipedia: 'I kept running'; OffGrid has him backtracking afterwards); a search helicopter passed without seeing him (Wikipedia, OffGrid); he sheltered in an abandoned Muslim shrine / marabout (all four); he ate bats there (all four) and drank or sucked their blood (Wikipedia, ExplorersWeb; OffGrid and History say only that he ate them raw); he then walked toward distant mountains in the early morning and evening (Wikipedia, OffGrid) eating beetles, lizards and snakes (Wikipedia; 'insects and reptiles' in History); he was found by a young girl tending goats, part of a Tuareg family who gave him goat's milk (Wikipedia, OffGrid; 'a young girl' in ExplorersWeb; History mentions only a village); he was in Algeria, 291 km / 181 miles off course (Wikipedia), 180 miles from where he disappeared (OffGrid, History), 'almost 300 km' (ExplorersWeb); he later returned to the race (six more times, 13th in 2001, per Wikipedia; 'completed the race in 2012' per OffGrid and History). Where the sources differ: (1) Age in 1994: 38 (Wikipedia, born July 1955) or 39 (OffGrid, History); no age is given in the film. (2) 'Pentathlete' (Wikipedia) or 'former Olympic pentathlete' (OffGrid); the film says only 'pentathlete'. (3) His race position: fourth (Wikipedia's narrative) or seventh (his own quote); not stated. (4) How long: he reached an oasis 'by the eighth day' and met the girl the next day (Wikipedia), 'after eight days' then the girl (OffGrid), 'for nine days he walked' (History), 'lost for nine days' (ExplorersWeb); the script says 'nine days later' and 'Day nine'. (5) Weight lost: 15 kg (Wikipedia), 35 lb (OffGrid, History), 18 kg (ExplorersWeb); no figure is given. (6) The helicopter is in Wikipedia (at sunset) and OffGrid (in the afternoon); the flare he fired at it is in Wikipedia only, so it appears on screen but is not narrated. (7) Rescue route: by camel to a village and then military police and a hospital in Tindouf (Wikipedia, OffGrid), 'an Algerian military camp' (ExplorersWeb), 'flown to a hospital' (History); the film stops at the tent. (8) The account is disputed: the race's founder, Patrick Bauer, called it a fabrication and 'physiologically impossible' (Men's Journal 1998, via Wikipedia and OffGrid) and some physiologists doubted it; against that, a 1995 film crew is reported to have found the shrine, his belongings and bat skeletons (Wikipedia, OffGrid) and Kamler's book concludes he did not lie (OffGrid). Because the bat detail rests on his own telling, the shot carries the label 'BY HIS OWN ACCOUNT' and the description says the story has been questioned. Left out on purpose: at the shrine he tried to end his life (all four sources); a Short for a general audience is not the place for it and nothing in the film alludes to it. Also left out: drinking his own urine (Wikipedia, OffGrid, History), the body of a holy man in the shrine (Wikipedia, from the BBC interview), the second aircraft and second storm, the blindfolded ride with military police, and the damage to his liver. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the runner (white cap, red pack, plain orange bib with no number or sponsor), the start arch, tents and marker flags (plain, no lettering or logos), the helicopter's colours, the shape of the shrine and its tower, the number of bats, the hand taking a bat, a lizard and a beetle (he ate them; how he caught them is not described), the hoof prints, the girl's and the older woman's clothes and the tent (sources say only a Tuareg girl, her grandmother and a tent), the bowl, the closing shot of him back on the start line, the steel flask Rook keeps (he carried water bottles; the flask is a stand-in), both maps (marked as sketches; the border and routes are not to scale), the six stage bars (only day four being the longest is sourced) and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet reviewed in three rounds with fixes after each (round 1: the sky rig was shadowing the whole desert and dunes were swallowing the camera in ten shots, so the sky was made invisible to shadow rays and every set got a dune-free stage; round 2: the hero dune sat on top of the storm stage and was moved north, the storm wall, shrine approach, bat close-up, girl and tent were restaged; round 3: spot fixes to the lizard and beetle shots), then one full-length low-resolution rehearsal (216x384, 4 samples, all 545 3D frames) composited with captions, HUD, overlays, inserts and sound and reviewed at three frames per shot; after that the inserts were re-laid out where captions covered them (runner file, stage bars, sun arc, sketch map) and the composite was rebuilt and checked again. The rehearsal passed the automated gate locally: 37 shots, mean 1.20 s, longest 1.88 s, loudness -15.0 LUFS, voice 12.3 dB over the bed, host in 16/37 shots (43%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.74. Every caption pair was measured against the frame width and the script was reworded where a pair was too wide; every HUD label fits. Audio was measured, not listened to. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud.
